blocks.x: This is Omar Simeon speaking. Where were you born? I was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, July 21st, 1902.
What is their rhythm or their style?

Well I would advise all the students on any instrument, I mean, to try to develop their own style of playing and their own tone. It doesn't necessarily mean, I mean, to play jazz, that you have to copy another man's style, or copy his tone, probably played 40, 50 years ago. So try to develop your own tone and your own style of playing. All the clarinets in New Orleans had different styles. Johnny's style was different than Jimmy's. All of them, they had their own individual style. So I would advise all the youngsters coming up, try to develop their own style of playing and their own tone.
And that's about all that you've got on. Can you tell us some more about your lessons with Teo and your counting and rhythm?

When I first started, Teo impressed, always impressed it. You had to keep your foot. For whole notes, four beats. For a half note, two beats. A quarter note, one beat. But I always had to keep that foot going while I was playing my exercises. I had to keep the foot going to keep it on time. And then later on after I started playing with the little bands around Chicago, then the drums. Then you've got the tempo and the beat from the drums. I mean the drums inspire you to play, you know. A drummer should push a soloist. I mean you should give them that drive. And he's very important. And a dance man, jazz man.
Can you tell us a little more about Teo? Did he play clarinet with you at the lessons? Did he have his instrument there to demonstrate, or did he do all of them?
Well, he always had his clarinet alongside him. And there were certain passages that I couldn't finger. He showed me how to finger that particular passage. He showed me which keys to press down.

Nobody seems to ever talk much about his style since he was quite early and didn't do much recording. I think he recorded a little bit with Piron. One of two sides. But what style did he play? What style did he play? Was it more like Noon or? More like Noon. More like than Dodds, I guess.
More so like Noon than Dodds.

Did he have a big tone as big as Noon or Dodds? They both had unusually big tones. Teo had a big tone. And others, people talk about that some of the older Creoles had more of a legitimate style, like symphony work, and they maybe played opera and all, but I didn't know if they really cut loose, you know, and really played a good style like, for instance, you and Dodds did. Did he really have the good improvised style though, or was it straight, more straight, do you think? Well, uh.
Did you hear him much in dance bands?
No, I never heard him much because I was a youngster.
Such a young kid. I wasn't allowed to go in the places where they played. But I just heard him, you know. And he did have a good warm, broad tone.
Yeah, very. Good broad tone. Good feeling, you know.
Yeah. Must have been a remarkable player from all the reports I've heard too.
I see something else coming. Can you tell me about the, you might say the role of the clarinet in the band, just what your job is?

Well, the trumpet carries the melodies, or they used to call, years ago, the syncopated melody, like a swing melody, you know. And the trombone, his range was below the trumpet, sort of in between the bass or baritone. Then the clarinet, the clarinet, the weave, used to weave in and out between the trumpet and trombone, you know. Variations.
That's variations on the melody, you know. Is it the chords? What do you think of this?
Yeah, a number's like a high society, you know. That's an example.

When you're playing and trying to make all those variations and all, do you think in your mind which chord you're playing is this B-flat chord? I'm going to F, I'm going to G, or do you think in your mind that?
No, it just comes natural.
Yeah, you don't try to think, well, I'm going to, this changes now to an F-card.
No, after you're familiar with the tune and familiar with the chord progressions.
Yeah, it's just in your mind and in your ear.

Which is very important too, chords, your different changes. That's very important too for a clarinetist. Because he's, he's up and down on the instrument, you know. And he has to keep in that particular chord. When it changes, or whether it holds over to another bar, he has to concentrate on that too. So after he's familiar with the tune, it comes natural. When he's familiar with all his chord changes.
Did you ever study any of the harmony? Did you ever play any on piano, try to pick out chords?
No, not very much.
You never had any lessons on that?
I used to just, you know, one finger, strike three, three notes. Chords.
Chords, yeah.
But I never did play piano much.
You think it's a good idea for clarinetists to learn it, or would you advise them to stick, spend the time they have on their own instrument?
Well, spend most of the time on my own particular instrument. Sometimes I go to the piano, figure out a chord, you know.
Would it be a good idea for clarinetists to learn a little bit about piano too, if they have time?
Well, it depends how far you want to go in music.
It's really necessary though, to be a good musician on the clarinetist.
No, it isn't necessary, because you can get familiar with the chords through the piano, and the banjo or guitar. Then it comes naturally. You just…

Another question about your early days, and your advice to students. Would you advise that they learn something about what they call sight singing, or ear training, first? Bunk Johnson, for instance, before his teacher let him pick up the carnet, he made him learn to sing the scales. And to train his ear, he had to do what they call sight singing, or like the do-re-mi-fasalati-do.
Yeah, well in those days they did, but now the modern style of teaching, they don't teach what they call a south-fage.
Yeah, south-fage.
I think most all the foreigners start that way, which is very good. But in this country they start you reading.
You didn't go through that yourself, the south-fage? No, I didn't. You started right on the instrument.
I started right on reading music. Well, one other question.
Why did you want to take up the clarinet? Why did you like that better than the others?
I just liked the particular instrument.
You don't remember when you first heard it was at the New Orleans bands, I guess, and you just liked it from back to the…
Yeah, I heard New Orleans and I, when we moved to Chicago, I heard Professor Dockett at this theatre. The theatre, so that's… And I liked the sound of the instrument.
Was that the Vendome, which…
No, this was the State.
The State, or…
Called the State Theatre. Yeah, I think that name was going around. Oh, yeah.

Have you had any suggestions for playing in smaller groups? If you don't have a full six or seven piece band, like the regular New Orleans band, if you've played a trio like the ones you did with Jelly, or if you have a job in a place with just the drummer and the piano or something, do you change your style?

Well, you don't change your style but first you introduce the melody. You get the melody established so that the people can know what you're playing. Then play solos you can improvise, play ad lib, whatever you want to. Then probably on the last chorus then you might, what we call, swing the melody. Swing lead. But in a group where there's a trumpet, then you don't have to concentrate on the melody, because the trumpet cares the melody. But just one wind instrument in the group, then the clarinetist has to play melody, variations, and everything else. Yeah.
In the band, like you talked about those last choruses, is there anything in particular you try to do? Do you try to go up higher for that last all-out chorus, or?
Well, usually you do on the last, when you reach a climax then you have to really drive that on the out choruses, what we call them on the last choruses.

Yeah. I remember some people have discussed, like Johnny Dodge used to sometimes stick to one register, play a whole solo in a low register. Maybe in the next chorus he'd play it in the upper register. Well, they say like noon, and I notice you do the same way, because you cover the whole instrument all over.
Yeah, in all registers, yeah. And usually on the last chorus then you, in your upper register then, your higher notes.

Did you ever try that style, just sticking to the low register for one chorus? Do you, I haven't heard you so much in recent years, to tell you the truth, I heard you last winter in New York, it's the last I've heard you.
On some solos I play in the lower register.
All the way through.

Play maybe one course in the lower register then, it depends on the amount of choruses that you're playing. You're playing two choruses or three choruses, then I usually play a chorus in the lower register, maybe one in the middle register and the last one in the upper register, when you reach the climax. But I very seldom play in one register. Usually I cover the whole instrument, you know. I like the letter T, T-U-T-U.
Did you ever practice much on your tonguing and legato and staccato styles?

Well, on staccato style, you pronounce the letter T, like T-U-T-U. Very sharp, quick stroke of the tongue. That's staccato playing. Then legato is more like da, like you would pronounce D-A. Da, da, da. That's legato.
Did you ever do any double tonguing in your dance work? Did you ever use that?
No, I never did do that on the clarinet or the saxophone. That was mostly done with brass instruments.
Yeah.

Tattaca, tetaca, tetaca. Yeah. Especially on trumpet. But in jazz is not necessary. You don't have occasion to use that. For clarinet, that's the double tonguing or tripletongue. Yeah. Just the staccato and legato toning. Yeah.
Can you tell us about developing your finger technique, any special exercises?
Well, it comes mostly from your scale work.
Just that you...
Your scale work, your scales and all the different keys.
Do you think a student ought to learn to transpose to be able to learn all those keys?
Well, it might probably help maybe in a studio or something like that at the last minute. But in just ordinary jazz, it's not as important as it would be in a pit orchestra.
Yet they should learn the different keys, I suppose. Of course, it would help them to learn how to transpose. I was going to ask a little bit about Oliver, when you joined King Oliver's band.

I joined Joe in 1927. We had a recording session just before we left Chicago. I think that was on the Brunswick label. Two of the numbers I remember recording was Willie the Weeper, which I used the soprano on that, soprano saxophone. Also used the clarinet and the alto saxophone. All three instruments on that particular arrangement.
Who else was in that band?

Bonnie B. Gard, on tenor, Kidd Ory, trombone, Paul Barberin, drums, Louis Russell, piano. And later on, when we reached St. Louis, Willie Foster joined the band. I think it was Pop Foster's brother. He joined us in St. Louis. Red Allen and Willie Foster. And Paul Barnes.
Oh yes, I met him.

On the alto sax. The three joined us in St. Louis. And from there we went to New York. We stayed around New York, what, a month, a couple of months or so. Played an engagement at the Savoy for two weeks. Then, after we finished the Savoy, Joe didn't have a very good booking agent. So it was really a struggle then, keeping the band together. And they started leaving, one by one, coming back to Chicago. I think Clarence Black was the first one to leave. Then Kidd Ory, and eventually Bonnie and I left. Then we joined Charlie Elger in Milwaukee. But the band didn't do so good in New York. Joe didn't have any advanced publicity.
Was he still playing pretty well then?
No, Joe was having trouble with his teeth then. So his children have, I mean, a good broad tone then.
Yeah, you played with Tate then for a while.

I played with Tate at the Metropolitan Theater. What? About 1928, 29, and 30. We played, well, legitimate music, you know, besides jazz. We did presentation work in the pit. And we played background music for the pictures. It was during the silent days then. So I got pretty familiar then with the different overtures and classical numbers.
Can you tell a bit about Heinz band when you were in quite a long time?

I joined Earl around 1931. I joined Earl about 1931 at the Grand Terrace Cafe then. A nightclub with a floor show. So we had to play dance music and also play music for the show. So anyone that wasn't familiar with reading music, there was no place for him in the band. Because we had to play show music. Sometimes we'd play part of an overture for a dance routine for the chorus. Of course, part of an overture like William Tell, a light cavalry, in the floor show. So if a musician couldn't read then he was lost, didn't have any job. And we played mostly, they called, during that time, special arrangements. Which were made by members of the orchestra, probably an outside arranger. Cecil Irwin was one of the arrangers when I joined the band. Then later on, Jimmy Mundy. And he has become quite a famous arranger now.
You traveled in front of the time too.
Well, we did mostly one-nighters and theatre engagements. Up to about 1937 when I left the band.
Do you prefer a small band playing a small band in a big one?
Well, in a small band, I mean, you have more liberties.
Would you rather play in a small or a large band?

Well, in a small band, you have a little more liberties. You can play what you want and the way you feel. And you get a lot of kicks playing in a small group. I mean, the type which I'm playing with now. But in the big band, you have to stick to the score until it comes to your solo that you can ad lib. But all during the arrangements, you have to stick to the score, you know. So that's the difference between the two bands. A little more liberty in a small band, a small group.
How many are in the Paris band now?
There are six now, the regular New Orleans instrumentation.
You never did play many jobs, did you, with smaller groups like trios? You had that trio you did with Naki once. What was that on the road?
Well, that was played at the University of Virginia in, I think, Charlottesville, Virginia. Only at jazz concerts, but mostly with the Six Beast group.
And the drummer Naki Parker.
And Arthur Herbert on drums.
There's one other question I might ask you, which is, sorry to put you on the spot too. Can you tell us anything about Jelly Roll? How do you like this style of playing?
Well, Jelly was very creative. And he came up during the ragtime era. So I guess you would call his style more towards the ragtime style, you know.
Was he easy to get along with, personally? Well, with us he was.
Yeah, we got along with him nicely. But with outsiders probably arguments would come up. But with all of us, the Red Hot Peppers, we got along very good with him.
The musicians that he understood and that he was trying to do. Yeah, that's right.
Did you hear Keppard?
Yeah, I played with Keppard for a while. How did you like him? At the Svobal with Charlie Elgin. Oh, he was a terrific drive, a trumpet player. He was a nice tone.
How did you compare him with Oliver, a different style in Oliver? Well he had a much, he had more drive than Oliver.
Big tone? Big tone, yeah.
Big tone, yeah. Big tone, yeah. And he could play very, very sweet too on his instrument. But he had that drive, you know, big, big, broad tone. More so, I think, than Oliver.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Well, Bunk was creative, but his tone was a little more subdued. He didn't have the drive or power that Keppard or Oliver or Louie had, but he was creative. More and more subdued tone, you know.
Any other favorite musicians you've had on different instruments? Trombone, did you hear Roy Palmer much?
Well I played with Roy on a few jobs around Chicago. He had a nice round tone.
Jelly said he was his favorite trombonist.
He was a very good musician too. He could transpose and play any part, clarinet part, trumpet part, or cello part, almost any part. Well.
Well. Well. . . . . . Thank you.

segments.title: Opening: Omer Simeon's birth in New Orleans
segments.summary: Simeon introduces himself and gives his birth place and date.

segments.title: Advice to students: develop your own tone and style
segments.summary: Simeon advises young players to find their own tone and style rather than copy others, noting New Orleans clarinetists each had a distinct style.

segments.title: Lessons with Tio: counting, keeping time, fingering
segments.summary: Tio made him keep his foot going to count note values; he demonstrated difficult fingerings on his own clarinet. Simeon also comments on drummers pushing a soloist.

segments.title: Tio's playing style and tone
segments.summary: Simeon says Tio sounded more like Noone than Dodds, with a warm broad tone, though he heard him little as a boy.

segments.title: The clarinet's role in the band and thinking in chords
segments.summary: Clarinet weaves variations between trumpet and trombone; chord changes come naturally once the tune is familiar.

segments.title: Piano and harmony study for clarinetists
segments.summary: Simeon never studied harmony or piano much, advises spending time on one's own instrument, though piano helps with chords.

segments.title: Solfege and ear training versus learning to read
segments.summary: Old teachers taught solfege first; Simeon started directly on reading music, as is common in this country.

segments.title: Why he chose the clarinet; hearing Professor Dockett in Chicago
segments.summary: He simply liked the instrument, heard clarinet in New Orleans and again at the State Theatre in Chicago after the family moved.

segments.title: Playing in small groups and the climax of the last chorus
segments.summary: In a small group, state the melody first, then improvise, then swing the last chorus; drive the out choruses.

segments.title: Using the registers of the clarinet in solos
segments.summary: Simeon covers the whole instrument, often moving from low to middle to upper register by the last chorus, like Noone.

segments.title: Tonguing: staccato, legato, no double tonguing
segments.summary: Explains staccato (T) and legato (D) tonguing and that double tonguing is a brass technique not needed in jazz clarinet.

segments.title: Finger technique, scales and transposing
segments.summary: Finger facility comes from scale work in all keys; transposing matters more in studio or pit work than in jazz.

segments.title: Joining King Oliver in 1927: personnel and the New York failure
segments.summary: Simeon joined Oliver in 1927 after a Brunswick session, names the band, describes the Savoy engagement, poor booking, members leaving, and Oliver's teeth trouble.

segments.title: With Erskine Tate at the Metropolitan Theater
segments.summary: He played about 1928-30 with Tate, doing legitimate presentation and silent-film background music in the pit.

segments.title: Earl Hines band at the Grand Terrace, 1931-37
segments.summary: Joined Hines around 1931 at the Grand Terrace; reading ability was essential for show music, with arrangers Cecil Irwin and Jimmy Mundy; one-nighters and theatres until 1937.

segments.title: Small band versus big band
segments.summary: Small groups allow more liberty; in a big band you stick to the score except for solos.

segments.title: His current six-piece band and a trio at Charlottesville
segments.summary: His current band uses the six-piece New Orleans instrumentation; a trio played at a University of Virginia jazz concert with Arthur Herbert on drums.

segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton: style and personality
segments.summary: Morton was creative, ragtime-rooted, and got along well with the Red Hot Peppers though he argued with outsiders.

segments.title: Comparing Keppard, Oliver and Bunk Johnson
segments.summary: Simeon played with Keppard at the Savoy under Charlie Elgar; Keppard had more drive and a bigger tone than Oliver, while Bunk was creative but more subdued.

segments.title: Trombonist Roy Palmer
segments.summary: Simeon played jobs with Palmer around Chicago and praises his round tone and ability to transpose and play any part.

segments.title: Closing thanks
segments.summary: The interview ends with thanks.
